title: Low-level cloud loss amplifies global warming, simulations suggest
excerpt: Low-level clouds over Earth's oceans play a prominent role in keeping our planet cool by reflecting sunlight away from the surface. But their response to climate change has been hard to model. Now, researchers at Caltech and Google have uncovered important insights into how clouds might respond to warming sea-surface temperatures and rising CO2 levels using a large dataset of simulations developed by the group.
content_html:
Low-level clouds over Earth's oceans play a prominent role in keeping our planet cool by reflecting sunlight away from the surface. But their response to climate change has been hard to model. Now, researchers at Caltech and Google have uncovered important insights into how clouds might respond to warming sea-surface temperatures and rising CO2 levels using a large dataset of simulations developed by the group.

"One of the largest open questions in climate prediction is how low clouds will respond to global warming," says Zhaoyi Shen, lead research scientist at Caltech's Ronald and Maxine Linde Center for Global Environmental Science and a co-author of a paper outlining the team's findings published July 24 in Science Advances. "Our results show potentially large, rapid adjustments of low clouds to high CO2 concentrations, which suggests Earth's climate might be more sensitive to high CO2 levels than some climate models currently project."

The team also found that the thinning of low clouds—uniform layers or large, lumpy expanses below 6,000 feet (1,800 meters) that cover massive portions of subtropical seas—amplifies global warming through a feedback loop: Rising sea-surface temperatures lead to fewer clouds, meaning less reflected sunlight and a warmer planet.

"This supports the growing body of evidence from the last few years," says Tapio Schneider, the Theodore Y. Wu Professor of Environmental Science and Engineering at Caltech and co-author of the paper; Schneider is also a principal scientist at Google. "We can now confidently rule out the idea that this effect is zero or that it somehow dampens global warming."

Resolving a stubborn cloud problem

While virtually all global climate models show that Earth is getting warmer, they differ widely in predictions of the exact long-term temperature rise triggered by sustained increases in atmospheric CO2. A large part of the challenge in reaching a scientific consensus has been the inability to resolve the fine-scale atmospheric turbulence that drives low-level cloud formation and dissipation.

By combining a modeling framework for simulations developed by Shen with the power of Google's computing resources, the research team used simulated large-scale weather data from a global climate model developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to drive thousands of high-resolution large-eddy simulations.

The simulations used atmospheric and surface-level conditions from 500 randomly selected locations across the tropical Pacific Ocean, taken during four different months to represent seasonal changes. Each location-season combination was then used to drive large-eddy simulations for four climate change scenarios: a 4°C sea-surface temperature increase from baseline; a quadrupling of atmospheric CO2 alone; a 4°C warming with doubled CO2; and a 4°C warming with quadrupled CO2.

Clouds react to CO2 itself

"We found that clouds respond directly to CO2 changes, a fact well understood in physics but perhaps a surprise to many," Schneider says. "Simply altering atmospheric CO2 shifts how infrared radiation moves through the air, directly affecting clouds even if temperatures are artificially held steady. Crucially, this effect is nonlinear; it accelerates as CO2 levels rise."

The team used more than 7,000 simulations in its investigation, a massive increase in sample size compared with earlier work. For example, an earlier study by Shen combined data from 500 simulations, which was itself an increase from the dozens of simulations in previous experiments.

The increase in scale was made computationally feasible using a large-eddy simulation code that leverages Google's tensor processing unit (TPU) clusters to build a robust collection of cloud states under different conditions. TPUs are specialized computer chips designed to accelerate artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning workloads.

"This experiment demonstrates the scale of computation made possible by Google's hardware capabilities," says Yi-Fan Chen, a software engineering director at Google and leader of the Google team that carried out the research. "It's computing at an extraordinary scale, demonstrating how processors originally developed for AI and machine learning can accelerate scientific discovery, enabling simulations that were previously out of reach."

A public resource for climate models

In addition to modeling the future, the dataset can help researchers elucidate the planet's past climates, such as during the Eocene Epoch (which began 56 million years ago and ended 33.9 million years ago), when CO2 levels were up to four times higher than today. Plus, the dataset is public, meaning anyone with a laptop can use it to build their own models.

"This new public dataset has the potential to help the broader scientific community evaluate and train turbulence, convection and cloud models for global climate models," says Shen. Shen is also part of the Climate Modeling Alliance (CliMA), a Caltech-based coalition of scientists, engineers and applied mathematicians from Caltech and MIT. "At the Climate Modeling Alliance, we are currently developing a new climate model designed to learn from data using AI and machine learning, and I am using this dataset to calibrate our model's new turbulence and convection schemes."

Schneider, who leads CliMA, says the group is already using the data extensively and that he is excited to see what others can glean from it.

"I hope researchers come up with new and creative ways of representing clouds in climate models and that we finally reduce these massive uncertainties in climate predictions," he says. "It's not going to happen overnight to change all sorts of climate models around the world, but over time, I think this can happen."

Publication details

content_html_zh:
地球海洋上空的低层云层通过反射太阳光远离地表，在保持地球凉爽方面发挥着重要作用。 但他们对气候变化的反应很难建模。 现在，加州理工学院和谷歌的研究人员利用该小组开发的大型模拟数据集，发现了云如何应对海面温度变暖和二氧化碳水平上升的重要见解。

加州理工学院罗纳德和玛克辛·林德全球环境科学中心的首席研究科学家、7 月 24 日发表在《科学进展》上的一篇概述该团队研究结果的论文合著者之一沉兆义表示：“气候预测中最大的开放问题是低云层将如何应对全球变暖。” “我们的结果显示，低云层可能对高二氧化碳浓度进行大规模、快速的调整，这表明地球气候可能对高二氧化碳浓度比目前一些气候模型预测的更敏感。”

研究小组还发现，低层云（覆盖亚热带海洋大部分地区的 6,000 英尺（1,800 米）以下的均匀层或大片、块状区域）的变薄会通过反馈循环加剧全球变暖：海面温度上升导致云层减少，意味着反射的阳光减少，地球变暖。

“这支持了过去几年越来越多的证据，”西奥多·Y·塔皮奥·施奈德 (Tapio Schneider) 说。 加州理工学院环境科学与工程教授、论文合著者吴教授；施耐德也是谷歌的首席科学家。 “我们现在可以自信地排除这种影响为零或它以某种方式抑制全球变暖的想法。”

解决顽固的云问题

尽管几乎所有全球气候模型都表明地球正在变暖，但它们对大气二氧化碳持续增加引发的长期气温上升的确切预测存在很大差异。 达成科学共识的很大一部分挑战是无法解决驱动低层云形成和消散的细尺度大气湍流。

通过将 Shen 开发的模拟建模框架与谷歌计算资源的强大功能相结合，研究团队使用来自美国国家海洋和大气管理局开发的全球气候模型的模拟大规模天气数据来驱动数千个高分辨率大涡流模拟。

模拟使用了热带太平洋上 500 个随机选择的地点的大气和地表条件，这些条件在四个不同的月份内进行，以代表季节变化。 然后使用每个地点-季节组合来驱动四种气候变化情景的大涡模拟：海面温度较基线升高 4°C；仅大气中的二氧化碳就增加了四倍；二氧化碳加倍，升温 4°C；以及用四倍的二氧化碳使气温升高 4°C。

云对二氧化碳本身有反应

施耐德说：“我们发现云层直接对二氧化碳的变化做出反应，这一事实在物理学中已广为人知，但可能令许多人感到惊讶。” “仅仅改变大气中的二氧化碳就会改变红外辐射在空气中的移动方式，即使人为地保持温度稳定，也会直接影响云层。 至关重要的是，这种效应是非线性的。随着二氧化碳浓度的上升，它会加速。”

该团队在调查中使用了 7,000 多次模拟，与早期的工作相比，样本量大幅增加。 例如，Shen 早期的一项研究结合了 500 次模拟的数据，这本身就是之前实验中数十次模拟的增加。

使用大涡模拟代码使规模的增加在计算上变得可行，该代码利用谷歌的张量处理单元（TPU）集群在不同条件下构建强大的云状态集合。 TPU 是专门的计算机芯片，旨在加速人工智能 (AI) 和机器学习工作负载。

“这个实验展示了谷歌硬件能力所实现的计算规模，”谷歌软件工程总监、进行这项研究的谷歌团队负责人陈一帆说。 “它的计算规模非常大，展示了最初为人工智能和机器学习开发的处理器如何加速科学发现，实现以前无法实现的模拟。”

气候模型的公共资源

除了对未来进行建模之外，该数据集还可以帮助研究人员阐明地球过去的气候，例如始新世时期（始于 5600 万年前，结束于 3390 万年前），当时的二氧化碳水平比今天高出四倍。 另外，该数据集是公开的，这意味着任何拥有笔记本电脑的人都可以使用它来构建自己的模型。

“这个新的公共数据集有潜力帮助更广泛的科学界评估和训练全球气候模型的湍流、对流和云模型，”沉说。 Shen 也是气候建模联盟 (CliMA) 的成员，该联盟是一个位于加州理工学院的联盟，由来自加州理工学院和麻省理工学院的科学家、工程师和应用数学家组成。 “在气候建模联盟，我们目前正在开发一种新的气候模型，旨在使用人工智能和机器学习从数据中学习，我正在使用这个数据集来校准我们模型的新湍流和对流方案。”

CliMA 的领导者施耐德表示，该小组已经广泛使用这些数据，他很高兴看到其他人可以从中收集到什么。

“我希望研究人员想出新的、创造性的方法来在气候模型中表示云，并最终减少气候预测中的巨大不确定性，”他说。 “改变世界各地各种气候模型不会在一夜之间发生，但随着时间的推移，我认为这可能会发生。”
